title: Data-Centre Bubble Talk: The Power of Overinvestment
abstract: Everyone is screaming about a bubble, but the real story is the electricity bill nobody wants to pay.
body:
## The Bubble That Isn't

I keep hearing the same tired refrain: data centres are a bubble, the AI boom is a mirage, and we are all going to wake up with a nasty hangover. It is a comforting story for people who missed the boat. But it is wrong. What we are watching is not a bubble. It is an overinvestment cycle, and the difference matters. A bubble is when everyone piles into an asset with no underlying value. An overinvestment cycle is when everyone piles into an asset with enormous underlying value, but they do it too fast, too stupidly, and with too much borrowed money. The value is real. The timing is a disaster. That is where we are with data centres.

The power grid is the tell. You cannot fake a substation. You cannot bluff a transmission line. When utilities in Virginia, Ireland, and Singapore start telling anyone who will listen that they cannot keep up, that is not hype. That is physics. The AI crowd has spent years talking about models and parameters and benchmarks. Now they are talking about megawatts. And megawatts are boring, expensive, and slow. That is why the bubble talk is so loud. It is easier to argue about valuations than to explain why your new campus will not have power until 2029.

## The Grid Is the Real Bottleneck

I have a friend who works for a utility in the American South. He is not a tech guy. He does not care about large language models. But he told me last month that his entire job has become managing a waiting list. Not for customers, but for power. Data centre developers are lining up like punters outside a casino, waving cash and begging for connections. And the utility is saying no. Not because they hate money, but because they cannot build fast enough. Transformers take years. Turbines take longer. And the people who make those things are not stupid. They have seen this movie before.

This is where the overinvestment becomes dangerous. The money is not the problem. There is plenty of money. The problem is that money cannot buy time. You can throw billions at a project and still wait four years for a switchgear. That gap between capital and capability is where fortunes get destroyed. It is also where the real opportunity lies. The companies that understand the grid, that have locked in power contracts, that have secured land with existing infrastructure, they will survive. The ones that assumed they could just plug in will not. I have no sympathy for them. They should have done their homework.

## The Japan Angle Nobody Talks About

Here is a contrarian take: the Bank of Japan is the most important player in this whole saga, and almost nobody is paying attention. For years, the BoJ has kept money cheap. That cheap money flowed everywhere, including into infrastructure projects that would never pencil out at normal rates. Now the BoJ is slowly, reluctantly, tightening. Not dramatically. Not like the Fed. But enough to matter. When the cost of capital rises, the marginal data centre project dies. And there are a lot of marginal projects out there.

I am not saying the BoJ will cause a crash. I am saying that the era of free money made people lazy. It made them build things that only work if interest rates stay at zero forever. That is not a business plan. That is a prayer. And prayers do not scale. The smart money is already repositioning. They are looking for assets that generate cash today, not in some hypothetical future where electricity is free and regulators are asleep. The dumb money is still buying the dip. Good luck to them.

## The Overinvestment Is the Point

Here is the thing that the bubble crowd misses: overinvestment is not a bug. It is a feature. Every major technology wave has been built on a mountain of wasted capital. The railways, the telegraph, the dot-com boom, the fibre glut of the late nineties. All of them involved too much money chasing too few good ideas. And all of them left behind infrastructure that the next generation used to build empires. The fibre that went bankrupt in 2001 became the backbone of the internet. The railways that went bust became the arteries of industrial economies. The data centres being built today, even the stupid ones, will be the foundation of whatever comes next.

That does not mean you should invest in every half-baked project. It means you should stop pretending this is a bubble. A bubble pops and leaves nothing. An overinvestment cycle leaves scars and assets. We are going to get both. The scars will be painful. The assets will be transformative. The trick is to be on the right side of that equation. And the right side is not the side that thinks power is free.

## What I Am Watching

I am watching the utilities. I am watching the transformer manufacturers. I am watching the companies that make the boring stuff that nobody tweets about. Switchgear. Cables. Cooling systems. The people who build the physical world are the ones who will decide who wins this race. Not the people who write blog posts about AGI. I am also watching the BoJ, because cheap money is the fuel that has kept this fire burning. When that fuel runs out, we will see who is swimming naked. My guess is a lot of people who thought they were wearing suits.

So no, I do not think we are in a bubble. I think we are in a gold rush, and the gold is electricity. The people selling shovels are going to get rich. The people digging are going to get tired. And the people who showed up late with a credit card and a dream are going to get exactly what they deserve. That is not a prediction. That is just how these things work. The power of overinvestment is that it builds the future, even when it destroys the investors. I will be watching from the sidelines, with a drink in my hand, waiting for the next round of fools to line up.
